History and sources
Concept
In the third century BCE, Archimedes bounded circumference divided by diameter using polygons.
Name
‘Pi’ names a Greek letter; the ratio was studied long before this name was adopted.
Symbol
Jones used π for this ratio in 1706; Euler popularized the notation in 1748.
E. B. Davies · Archimedes’ calculations of square roots (2011)

Research on bounds for √3 in Archimedes’ Measurement of a Circle; how he obtained them remains uncertain.

Second-edition scan: survey in ch. II; interpretation of 7:22 and 14:11 in ch. IX, p. 93 (PDF 106). A later author’s theory, not a record of builders’ intent.

History and sources
Concept
Euler studied the difference between 1+1/2+…+1/n and ln n in 1734–35; the work appeared in 1740.
Name
The name commemorates Euler and Mascheroni’s later calculations in 1790.
Symbol
Euler wrote C, Mascheroni A. γ is attested in the nineteenth century; priority for its use is disputed.

History and sources
Concept
Archimedes used bounds 265/153 < √3 < 1351/780 in Measurement of a Circle; how he obtained them is uncertain.
Name
‘Square root of 3’ describes the positive number whose square is 3; it is not named after a discoverer.
Symbol
√ appears in Rudolff’s Coss (1525), long after Archimedes’ calculations.
E. B. Davies · Archimedes’ calculations of square roots (2011)

Research on bounds for √3 in Archimedes’ Measurement of a Circle; how he obtained them remains uncertain.

Coss (1525): use of √. This dates notation, not the discovery of every square root.

History and sources
Concept
Book X of Euclid’s Elements studies commensurability of lengths and squares, the context of modern irrational roots.
Name
‘Square root of 6’ denotes the positive number with square 6. A separate discovery date has not been established.
Symbol
√6 combines the radical sign, attested in Rudolff in 1525, with the number 6.
Euklides / D. Joyce · Elements X.9

Commensurability of lengths and squares: ancient context for modern irrational roots.

History and sources
Concept
Old Babylonian tablet YBC 7289 contains an accurate approximation to a square’s diagonal, today’s √2.
Name
‘Square root of 2’ is an algebraic description. The tablet does not use this modern name.
Symbol
Modern √2 uses the radical sign in Rudolff’s tradition (1525); the tablet uses sexagesimal notation.
D. Melville · YBC 7289, Yale Babylonian Collection

Old Babylonian tablet with an approximation to √2; not evidence about the builders at Giza.

History and sources
Concept
Euclid’s construction II.11 divides a segment in a ratio now expressed using √5 and the golden ratio.
Name
‘Square root of 5’ describes a number with square 5: modern algebraic language for ancient geometry.
Symbol
√5 uses the radical sign attested in Rudolff (1525), rather than Euclid’s notation.
Euklides / D. Joyce · Elements II.11

A construction dividing a segment; modern algebra relates it to √5 and φ.

History and sources
Concept
The sequence sums three preceding terms. Feinberg described it in Fibonacci–Tribonacci in 1963.
Name
The article’s title documents ‘Tribonacci’, referring to Fibonacci and three summands.
Symbol
T is this app’s abbreviation for the constant, not evidence of a universal historical symbol.
M. Feinberg · Fibonacci–Tribonacci (1963), pp. 71–74

Original article documents the name and recurrence summing three preceding terms; not priority for every such recurrence.

History and sources
Concept
In 1919 Brun proved convergence of the reciprocal twin-prime sum, e.g. (1/3+1/5)+(1/5+1/7)+….
Name
‘Brun’s constant’ commemorates Viggo Brun and denotes that sum, rather than an edge length.
Symbol
Here B₂ denotes the twin-prime sum. It differs from B, the pyramid’s base side.
MacTutor · Viggo Brun

The 1919 convergence theorem for reciprocal twin primes and the constant’s name.

Provenance of the adopted estimate 1.902160583104; not all its digits are established.

History and sources
Concept
In a 1597 letter to Kepler, Mästlin gave about 0.6180340 for the longer part of a unit segment divided in the golden ratio.
Name
‘Inverse φ’ describes the same proportion in the opposite direction, not a new discovery.
Symbol
1/φ combines division with the later symbol φ; we do not attribute ancient origins to this notation.
J. O’Connor, E. Robertson · MacTutor: Golden ratio

Mästlin (1597): 0.6180340; ‘golden section’ attested in Ohm (1835), its originator unknown.

History and sources
Concept
Euclid VI, definition 3, describes extreme and mean ratio: whole to larger part as larger to smaller.
Name
‘Golden section’ is attested in Martin Ohm in 1835; its originator has not been established.
Symbol
Cook in 1914 credits Mark Barr with proposing φ. This documents notation, not use of the ratio by Phidias.
Euklides / D. Joyce · Elements VI, Definition 3

Definition of division in extreme and mean ratio, without the name ‘golden’ or symbol φ.

History and sources
Concept
Studies of logarithms and compound interest led to e. Bernoulli studied the limit of (1+1/n)ⁿ in 1683.
Name
‘Euler’s number’ commemorates the mathematician, not evidence that the concept began with him.
Symbol
Euler used e in a 1727–28 manuscript and in print in Mechanica (1736). Why he chose the letter is uncertain.

Logarithms and compound interest; Bernoulli studied the limit of (1+1/n)ⁿ in 1683.

History and sources
Concept
e−1 subtracts one from e. Its historical context is the development of logarithms and the exponential function.
Name
‘e minus one’ describes an operation; no separate historical name or discovery has been established.
Symbol
e−1 combines Euler’s symbol with subtraction. It differs from e⁻¹, which means 1/e.

History and sources
Concept
Christian Lange describes a modern golden-oval proposal: a plane cuts a hyperbola’s surface of revolution, with Z₀=7.65.
Name
‘Golden Egg’ names the proposal and preset; its first use or ancient origin has not been established.
Symbol
L/W means length divided by width. Target φ is an existing constant, not a new L/W constant.
Christian Lange · The golden angle (June 2002)

Author’s source for the modern ‘golden egg’, zr=1 and Z₀=7.65 proposal. It does not establish its physical claims or builders’ intent; a separate audit checks the numbers.

Definition of division in extreme and mean ratio, without the name ‘golden’ or symbol φ.

Pojęcie
Archimedes w III w. p.n.e. ograniczył stosunek obwodu koła do średnicy za pomocą wielokątów.
Nazwa
„Pi” jest nazwą greckiej litery; stosunek badano długo przed przyjęciem tej nazwy.
Symbol
Jones użył π dla tego stosunku w 1706 r.; Euler upowszechnił zapis w 1748 r.

Badanie granic √3 w Pomiarze koła Archimedesa; metoda ich uzyskania pozostaje niepewna.

„Pierwiastek z 6” oznacza dodatnią liczbę o kwadracie 6. Nie ustalono osobnego momentu jej odkrycia.
Symbol
√6 łączy znak pierwiastka, poświadczony u Rudolffa w 1525 r., z liczbą 6.

Nazwa
„Pierwiastek z 2” to opis algebraiczny. Tabliczka nie używa tej współczesnej nazwy.
Symbol
Współczesne √2 używa znaku √ z tradycji Rudolffa (1525); tabliczka ma zapis sześćdziesiątkowy.

Konstrukcja Euklidesa II.11 dzieli odcinek w proporcji dziś wyrażanej przez √5 i złotą liczbę.
Nazwa
„Pierwiastek z 5” opisuje liczbę o kwadracie 5. To współczesny język algebraiczny dla dawnej geometrii.
Symbol
√5 używa znaku √ poświadczonego u Rudolffa (1525), a nie zapisu Euklidesa.

Nazwa
Tytuł artykułu dokumentuje nazwę „Tribonacci”, nawiązującą do Fibonacciego i trzech składników.
Symbol
T jest skrótem użytym w tej aplikacji dla stałej, nie dowodem uniwersalnego historycznego oznaczenia.

Pojęcie
Brun w 1919 r. dowiódł zbieżności sumy odwrotności liczb pierwszych bliźniaczych, np. (1/3+1/5)+(1/5+1/7)+….
Nazwa
„Stała Bruna” upamiętnia Vigga Bruna i dotyczy tej sumy, a nie długości krawędzi.
Symbol
B₂ oznacza tutaj sumę dla par bliźniaczych. To inne B niż bok podstawy piramidy.

e−1 powstaje przez odjęcie jedności od e. Jego kontekst historyczny to rozwój logarytmów i funkcji wykładniczej.

„e minus jeden” jest opisem działania; nie ustalono odrębnej historycznej nazwy ani odkrycia.
Symbol
e−1 łączy symbol Eulera z odejmowaniem. To nie e⁻¹, które oznacza 1/e.
